text: I guess the short answer is that Cassini, built and launched from Earth, carries Earth microbes. If a gravity assist went wrong, it could hit Enceladus or another moon, the real fear being that a potentially habitable moon gets seeded with terrestrial life. So the team planned the Grand Finale, a controlled plunge into Saturn’s atmosphere, where the craft would be destroyed. It saved fuel and gave close planetary data, but the contamination worry was about keeping Earth life out of a moon that might have its own. Saturn itself is gas, so it doesn’t need the same care.

I never really got why the non-pumping leg would be the one complaining. You hold one foot down while the other swings and pushes, so the stationary leg is doing a lot of quiet work you don’t think about. Your hip stays bent and pulled inward while the other leg does the pumping, so the adductors and hip flexors end up bracing isometrically against the board and your body weight. That constant bracing is tiring and can make those muscles ache.

But why does that matter? If you’re always pumping with one leg, the bracing side gets overloaded. Your hip is held in the same bent angle, and if your form isn’t clean, your knee or foot can be under stress. I’d check whether the pain is more in the hip crease or inner thigh. If it’s there, it’s likely those bracing muscles. If it’s at the knee, your stance width or knee alignment might be off.

Honestly I always assumed the pumping leg should be the sore one, but no, the holding leg can be the complaint. Try shifting your stance a little wider or narrower to see if that changes things. When you’re stopping or landing, that stationary leg also takes the impact. A board is slippery, so you’re relying on it to keep you upright. That’s a lot of work for a muscle group that’s basically just holding position.

Honestly I never got why people get tripped up by this. Calling them "African American" isn't a claim that they just landed in New York or Boston yesterday. It's a marker of where the ancestors came from. The trans-Atlantic slave trade moved millions of people from the western and central coastlines of Africa to the Americas. So yeah, most Black Americans weren't born on the African continent, but their bloodlines are deeply rooted there. But why does that matter? It gives a shared historical and cultural anchor. It's a way to group a massive, diverse population whose ancestors were historically scattered across the continent. I guess you can use other terms, but "African American" just points to that deep historical connection instead of a simple passport check. I mean, if someone was born in Chicago, they are still part of that broader diaspora. The term isn't a residency requirement. I don't think the label is meant to be a literal geography test. It just recognizes the forced migration that shaped the modern demographic. I'd say it's the best umbrella term we have for that specific history. People keep treating it like a birthplace rule, which I think is a mistake.

I guess the short answer is that Syria doesn't just have one arms pipeline. Government forces lean on state arsenals, captured stockpiles, and support from allies. Rebel groups mostly get small arms and explosives through neighbouring border crossings, regional suppliers, and battlefield captures. I mean, you see people carrying rifles when there's supposed to be quiet. Why still? Because on the ground nobody feels safe enough to put guns down. A truce can break overnight, so both sides keep buying or smuggling what they need. It's not as if anyone trusts the other side not to stab them in the back.

Honestly I never got why people lump every drug into the same bad basket, because the difference is usually dose, duration, and what exactly the drug does, not just "drug" in the abstract. You can take a drug for a short time and feel fine, and you can take a different drug for years and end up in a hole, so "all drugs are bad" is a bit of a myth. The question that actually matters is, why does intense pleasure usually come with some price?

Because the brain's reward system isn't a vending machine you can keep pulling from. If something makes you feel great, the brain notices and tries to restore balance. That's tolerance in the most basic sense: the same hit stops feeling as strong, so you want more, or you start feeling flat between doses. With something like heroin or cocaine, the pleasure is so strong that the rebound is also so strong, and the body gets dragged along. So the "zero adverse effects" version is rare, not because pleasure is magic, but because the same neurochemistry that makes it pleasurable is what makes the brain adapt to it.

But why does that matter? Because the adverse effects aren't a separate tax on top of the good stuff; they're built into the mechanism. A drug that floods the reward system hard will almost always make the system compensate. The pleasant peak and the crash aren't independent things. That's why a drug that gives intense euphoria with literally zero downsides would be unusual, and I guess I'd be surprised by it.

Still, I mean, it doesn't have to be all or nothing. Some drugs hit the reward system gently and are more about steadiness, and those can be used for a while without the same wild swings. The problem starts when the effect is intense and the use is long or heavy. So if you're after that strong high, you're already in the part of the risk curve where adverse effects show up more, whether in the body or the mind.

Hi Mark,
It’s real, and I’m not the only one who gets it. I guess shopping can trigger that ache because your body is dealing with stress, crowds, poor posture, too little water or food, and staring at prices. If you stand or walk a lot, your back, legs, or shoulders tighten, and the tension can creep into your head. But why does that matter? Honestly I never got why it isn’t just a normal headache. It isn’t: it’s your body telling you it’s been overworked. Try sipping water, sitting, and finding a quiet corner. If it bothers you, tell a GP or physio.
Cheers,
Jon

Hi Maya,
Thanks for asking. I think your brain simply went with the strongest connection it had for cow and milk. They hang together in language, so the answer jumped out before you could catch yourself. But why does that association win? Because language glues certain words together, and under distraction the most available word tends to come out first. The silk repetition probably made things noisier, so that little trick question slipped you. Cows drink water. Calf milk isn't the same as cow water, but your answer made a kind of sense. Don't beat yourself up. I mean, it wasn't a memory failure. Your attention was scrambled by repeating silk, and the question was loaded. He was probably enjoying a small gotcha. The fact that cows drink water is just the correct answer; your brain answered with the nearest related word. That's normal, not a sign of trouble.
Take care,
Leo

Hi Sam,

Thanks for the email. I know you are in a hurry, so here is the short version. If you are buying a house, the two things that matter most are the price and what the mortgage will actually cost you over time. The sticker price is not the whole story. Taxes, insurance, maintenance, and any repair bills can quietly add thousands.

I mean, people get so focused on the open house tour and forget to read the fine print. Get the purchase agreement and mortgage offer in writing before you agree to anything. If you cannot understand a clause, ask the lender or lawyer what it means.

Don’t rush the valuation. A survey of the building can surface roof, damp, or structural problems. That is the part I would not skip, honestly. Also, if the seller is willing, negotiate the price down before the mortgage is fixed. A lower price usually means a lower monthly payment, and that is a real win.

One quick test: can you cover the mortgage payment for six months if your income drops? If not, the deal is riskier than it looks.

Let me know what questions you had in mind.

All the best,
Alex

Hi Alex,

Yeah, that 3-in-1 question tripped me up too. The short version is that a 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner is still a hair-focused formula: it cleanses and leaves conditioning film on hair. The 3-in-1 adds the bodywash angle, so the same liquid is meant to be used on skin and hair. That means the cleansers are usually milder, and there may be extra moisturizing bits aimed at the body. But that is mostly a convenience claim. In practice, I’d call a 3-in-1 a compromise formula, good for quick all-purpose washing, not as strong as a dedicated shampoo, conditioner, and bodywash. If your hair or skin needs serious care, separate products usually do better. I don’t think there’s some hidden ingredient that makes the 3-in-1 genuinely superior. It’s mainly one bottle doing several jobs, and the trade-off is specificity.

It’s also worth saying the name itself is doing a lot of work: the “3-in-1” bit is selling convenience, not necessarily performance. If you’re traveling or want fewer bottles, it can be handy. But if you care about soft hair or very dry skin, I’d still choose separate products, because the combined formula has to stay mild enough for both.

Let me know if that makes sense.

Cheers,
Me

Hey Sam,

Good question. I guess you're thinking about plate tectonics, but measuring a whole continent moving is not something you can see. We actually have two main ways.

The modern way is GPS. Surveyors put receivers on bedrock and check positions over months or years. By comparing where the receivers were earlier with where they are now, you get a speed. It's not a single measurement, you need a network of points and time.

Then there are older clues. Fossils in different places, matching rock formations, and magnetic stripes on the seafloor all suggest past motion. They don't give you a simple speed for a whole continent, but they show continents used to sit differently.

I mean, if you put a GPS point on, say, the bedrock of a continent and a point on another continent and watch the distance grow or shrink, that's how you get a rate. You can also use the motion of tectonic plates from those points.

So it's really a combination of precise positioning plus geology. I never got why it felt so impossible to measure, but now it's just a matter of careful surveying and comparing.

Hope that makes sense.

Cheers,
Me

I guess the short version is that inbreeding raises the odds that two copies of the same bad recessive allele meet in one child. IQ isn't one gene; it's shaped by many small-effect genes and environmental factors. When relatives share more DNA, kids end up with more matching gene copies, so harmful recessive mutations that sit hidden in carriers can show up.

In other words, inbreeding doesn't subtract IQ points directly; it changes the odds of hidden genetic flaws becoming visible. But that's not a law that every inbred child ends up below average. It's a probability shift: more recessive load, lower expected cognitive scores on average. So the 'significantly lower' comes from population studies that pool those risks and environmental confounds, not from a single inbreeding 'IQ gene'. My honest take: call it a genetic-load issue. Still, the science is about more matching gene copies exposing rare damaging variants, which can drag cognitive ability down.

I honestly never got why an arm injury feels less bad. I guess there’s something to it, but I’m not really sure the whole body has the same pain level everywhere. The arm has plenty of nerves, so it’s not numb. What might matter more is that injuries higher up near the shoulder or torso hit areas with more important things going on, and the arm can absorb a lot before it starts to really bug you. A shot to the arm is annoying and can be serious, but you probably keep going. Same with a cut or a knock. That said, if you get hit hard enough anywhere, it hurts enough that you’ll stop what you’re doing.

Here’s the short answer: carbon monoxide steals the oxygen-carrying job from blood, while carbon dioxide is mostly the body’s waste gas. Carbon monoxide does not make the air feel stale. It slips into the same space in hemoglobin where oxygen sits, and it clings far more tightly than oxygen does. Oxygen swaps in and out quickly, but carbon monoxide makes a long-stay tenant. That reduces how much oxygen reaches tissues. The brain and heart get starved even if the room still has plenty of oxygen. That is why CO can be deadly when the air smells completely normal.

Why isn’t carbon dioxide equally bad? It is not “harmless”; at high levels it can displace oxygen and make breathing feel uncomfortable. But at everyday indoor levels, your body expects CO2 and handles it. The difference is molecular chemistry, not just the amount of gas in the room. CO binds the iron in hemoglobin with roughly two hundred times the affinity of oxygen; exact numbers vary with conditions, so I would not put a single precise multiple on the wiki unless a source gives one. The point is that it blocks oxygen transport, not that it directly poisons tissues by itself.

I never quite got why people overreact to the CO2 side, because in normal workspaces it is mostly regulated by your breathing. CO is the sneaky one: colourless, almost odourless, and it can build up when combustion is incomplete or ventilation is poor. For a new colleague, the practical warning is that CO needs to be caught early, because symptoms like headache or nausea can be confused with tiredness. The real risk is silent oxygen starvation, and that is why a CO alarm, not a smell test, is what you should rely on.

I guess the real reason we learn that position is to keep our heads and chests from slamming into the seat or floor during a hard stop or ditching. That is the part that matters.

I mean, it is less about looking disciplined and more about giving your body somewhere safe to hit. You sit close to the back of the seat, knees forward, head down, and put your hands where they can shield your face or grip the armrests. And if you cannot reach the armrests, you tuck your hands over your face.

But why does that matter? Because during a sudden deceleration, your body wants to lurch forward. The brace gives that forward motion a controlled stop. It also protects the head from the seat in front, which is often the most damaging contact. Still, the exact hand placement varies by aircraft, so the cabin crew tells you what they need.

Honestly, I never got why everyone learns it without thinking, but once you see it as a way to stop your own body safely, it makes sense. In the aisle seat I just keep my hands over my face.

I guess the short answer is just scale. I mean, before factories, a business was a local baker or a village smith. They couldn't mass produce, so they stayed local. But why does that matter? Because to be a global name, you need to make ten thousand identical things. And without machines, you can only make what your hands can do. Still, an old family bakery might be famous in its own town, but it isn't a brand people recognize everywhere. So pre-industrial businesses were too small and too personal to become global household names. I think that's really why we don't have famous pre-industrial companies.

I never got why people rush to the dealership when the numbers rarely make sense. My friend bought a car through a local bank last month and saved over two thousand dollars compared to the dealer's offer, even though the dealer was advertising 0% financing. That’s not just luck.

The trick is that dealers often advertise low or zero percent rates, but they usually do this on a higher price. Say the car’s base price is $30,000. The dealer might say “0% on $25,000 after a $5,000 down payment.” That sounds great, but their car price is usually inflated. A bank might charge 5% on the full amount, yet if they buy the same car for $32,000 while the dealer quotes $35,000, the lower price at the bank can offset the higher rate.

Take a four-year loan. At the dealer, the loan is $25,000 at 0%, so total paid is just the principal. At the bank, borrowing $27,000 (after the same down payment) at 5% means paying roughly $3,500 in interest. But the dealer’s car is $3,000 more expensive, and they almost always add fees and packages. When you add those in, the bank’s total cost comes out lower.

The 0% deals are usually short-term or conditional, and the price gap swallows the savings. A bank is cheaper when you compare total cost of ownership, not just the interest rate. I’d check the out-the-door price at both places, then run the total over the full loan term. That’s the only way to see what you’ll actually pay.

I’m not saying dealers always rip you off, but the math often works against them. You’re paying for the convenience of one-stop shopping. If you can take time to compare the full price, a bank usually wins.

I've been trying to explain to people that legalizing marijuana in the US isn't one big switch. Different states make different choices, and those choices can decide whether you get a green light or a red one on your license. In Colorado, for example, a person can buy flower in a dispensary and take it home, but driving under the influence is still the same standard as alcohol, and a failed field sobriety test can cost you your license. New Jersey has a medical program, but the list of qualifying conditions is narrower than people expect, and the paperwork takes months. My take is simple: legality is real only inside each state's borders. If your state hasn't legalized it, your neighbor's dispensary doesn't make it legal for you. That's the part that confuses most people. I still think more states will legalize eventually. I just think people should stop assuming one state's law saves another.

I hear "your body runs on electricity" and I roll my eyes, but I don't want to be too snarky about it, because the ion thing really is the answer. Nerves fire by swapping sodium and potassium ions across the cell membrane, and that movement is the spark. The heart uses the same trick to make its rhythm. Honestly I never got why people make it sound like a battery when it's really just charged particles shuffling side to side.

I guess what surprises me is how little music a sampler actually uses. I mean, you don't just drop the whole chorus in. You pull a two second drum break, loop it, pitch it down, lay it under a new bassline, and suddenly you have something that feels old and new at the same time. But why does that matter? Because a tiny slice of a 1970s record can carry the whole mood of the decade. That's the trick. I've watched people in DAWs or on an MPC cut a vocal fragment so cleanly that the original singer's phrasing survives the chop, and I keep thinking this is closer to editing than composition.

Honest question: I never got why people think sampling is lazy. You have to choose, cut, clean up, time-stretch, and often get clearance. If the slice comes from a recording you didn't make, you need permission or pay. That's the unglamorous part nobody talks about. I've seen a beat start life as a chopped vocal from an obscure soul record, then get pitched, reversed, and buried under a kick drum. The original singer probably has no idea their voice is now under a grunge track. Still, the feeling survives the cut.

So I think sampling is less about copying and more about stealing a moment. You take the part that hits you and make it the foundation. The rest of the song becomes your conversation with that fragment. You might loop a hi-hat, then bury a muted guitar stab behind it, then add your own percussion on top. The sample doesn't need to dominate. If it does, you've probably lost the point.

And that's why a sampled break can feel more real than a freshly recorded beat. It brings history into the mix. A fresh drum loop is sterile. A chopped groove carries dirt. The beat starts with the memory and then you build around it, not over it. I don't think the musician is making a whole new song. They're making a room for the old moment to sit.

My rule is simple: if the sample fights the beat, change the beat, not the memory. The best samples sound inevitable. They don't announce themselves. If you have to hear "oh, that's from the old Motown record", you've overdone it. I'd rather hear a half-remembered fragment than a recognizable quote. That's the difference between borrowing a feeling and borrowing a melody.

I keep blaming my skull, but honestly a headache is not my head hurting. I think it is more like a pressure alarm. Last week I skipped water and stared at screens for nine hours; by evening my temples were throbbing, and my neck felt tight. The pain isn't a sign that something is broken; it is the nervous system and blood vessels responding to strain. I guess the body is trying to get attention, like a red light rather than a broken engine. I am not a doctor, but the detail I care about is that headaches often come from things you can fix: bad sleep, tight neck, eyes doing too much work. My position is simple: stop waiting for a pill. First I get water, lie in the dark, and roll my shoulders. If it does not ease in an hour, then I call a doctor.

I can't even tell you if the food was good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday. We chose this place because we had a 10 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought it would be easy. We put our names on their completely useless digital waitlist. They told us to come back at 8:23 p.m. to pay. We did, but then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually said we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15! We were just two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, say it up front so our night isn't a complete waste. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

I went Friday around 4:30 p.m. and there wasn’t a single line, which took me by surprise. The two of us ended up paying around $130. That felt steep. Before going in, I expected the price to be comparable to a steakhouse, and afterward I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than I thought a steakhouse would.

Honestly, I was disappointed there wasn’t any steak. At that price I assumed we’d at least get some kind of steak option. The meats were lamb, prime rib, and chicken, and I can get those at other Las Vegas buffets for much less.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are all over Vegas buffets, but rock crab claws were new to me, and that was interesting. The catch was no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next one that I didn’t want shells flying at the people beside us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station wasn’t especially distinctive. It reminded me quite a bit of the Rampart Casino buffet. Dessert had gelato and pastries, but nothing stood out. There were also fresh juices, though I didn’t try any.

I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If there’s no wait, it’s worth trying once. But if the line is long, I’d probably think twice.

★★★★☆ Keeping it

The spacebar rattles. Hit it with the edge of my thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under my finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been stuck without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays right on the desk, and I just tap the spacebar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, at least the under-21 version, so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. A few individual acts are impressive too, like the strength stuff, the aerialists, and the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not exactly a rip-off, just if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still really don’t know. A dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, too much is happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal for $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

Approximately two years ago, I ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. The shirts never arrived because the sales rep wrote down the delivery address wrong: her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. The address should have been 5407, but the package went to 5401. The residents at 5401 took it to the local UPS store for return. The package disappeared and was never seen or heard from again. We didn't learn about it until several weeks later. During the dispute, we placed an additional order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. Then the owner handled it. He acknowledged the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He claimed we were partly responsible because we had not been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually received a credit.
